items.text:
How we helped our puppy with seperation anxiety and can now happily leave her for up to 4 hours, 6 hours absolute max in an emergency etc and she is fine!

Seperation anxiety is a huge struggle for Vizslas so it was a lot of work for us to get to this point! We are not trainers but a few of you have been asking so this is just some of the stuff we did! 

1. Picking up and dropping keys regularly so the sound wasn’t a trigger 

2. Crate drills - treats in crate, let out crate, shuttting door etc and extending the time 

3. Doors a bore drill - opening and shutting door, extending to leaving house etc 

4. Treats while we were gone, ignored when we got in

5. Crate training - put in while I work and while we sleep to make it her comfy downtime space 

6. Commit to it and not let it stop us from living our lives! 

#seperationanxiety #seperationanxietytraining #vizsla #puppytraining #howtoleavepuppyathome

items.text:
Timing is everything in separation anxiety training, and it’s more than just how long you leave your dog alone.
Getting the timing right can make training easier for both you and your dog, and it’s key to building confident, relaxed alone time. Here’s what to consider:
1️⃣ Time of day matters
Train when your dog is naturally calm and settled. Make sure their needs have been met, and that external distractions, like noisy neighbours or household activity, are minimal. Training when your dog is already stressed or overexcited can make sessions harder and slow progress.
2️⃣ Timing of repetitions
Your dog needs time to fully relax before the next repetition. I usually recommend a short break of 20–60 seconds, but this will vary depending on your dog, some may need longer.
3️⃣ Timing of duration increases
Only increase the target duration in your next training session after a successful session where your dog remained calm and relaxed.
4️⃣ Warm-ups and target duration
Warm-ups ease your dog into training and allow multiple positive exposures to being alone in one session. Keep warm-ups much shorter than your target duration, a common mistake is making warm-ups too long, which can increase stress before the main session even begins.
5️⃣ Timing of returning early
Sometimes your dog may start showing subtle signs of stress during a session. Recognising these signals and returning earlier than planned prevents overloading them, reduces anxiety, and helps your dog associate alone time with calm, positive experiences.
Timing isn’t just a detail, it’s a foundation for successful separation anxiety training. Pay attention to these cues, and your dog will learn faster, stay calmer, and build confidence more reliably.
If you’re unsure how to structure sessions around your dog’s ideal timing, or want personalised guidance for your dog’s separation anxiety, book a free call via the link in my bio.

items.text:
“Just let them cry it out” is one of the most common pieces of separation anxiety advice online… but it can actually make things worse.

When a dog is panicking after being left alone, they aren’t being dramatic they’re experiencing genuine distress. Repeatedly pushing them beyond what they can cope with can reinforce the fear and make home alone time feel even more unsafe.

Instead, we want to create positive, manageable experiences at a pace they can cope with to help build confidence over time. 

And if you’ve tried the “cry it out” method before there’s absolutely NO judgement from me. I tried it too before I understood separation anxiety better. It’s incredibly overwhelming trying to navigate all the conflicting advice online, know what to trust and know what’s best for your dog. 

That’s why I created a FREE guide which covers why common advice you’ve already tried hasn’t worked. comment “guide” and I’ll send my free guide straight to your inbox 💫

The method that has the best results, the highest chance of actually treating the issue, and is also the most humane option, is without a doubt systematic desensitization. But desensitization is NOT just “start small and gradually raise the difficulty” - your dog is going to catch on to that really quickly and probably start getting very stressed out. This is a process that needs to be done intentionally, carefully, and ideally with a strong knowledge base to guide you.

How do you teach a dog with separation anxiety that being alone is safe when they start panicking the second you’re out of sight - or worse, they’re already panicking while you’re getting ready to leave?

One way to get started is to simply remove those pre-departure cues - keys, coats, shoes - just step outside for a second or two without them! We can add them in systematically later, but this helps us get right at the root of why your dog is anxious - being alone.
